data.content_ref: inline:Popper's position smuggles in induction through the back door by relying on a hidden uniformity principle: that the future will resemble the past regarding test outcomes. If a scientist prefers Theory A over Theory B solely because A survived tests that B failed, they are implicitly assuming that the conditions which allowed A to survive will persist, which is an inductive leap. The cost of accepting this view is the collapse of Popper's distinct 'critical rationalism' into a disguised form of Bayesianism or standard inductivism, stripping his philosophy of its unique claim to solve the problem of induction.
